blocks.title: File I/O
bullets: Up until now, everything we've programmed has stored information in memory. Once the program ends, all information gathered is lost.
File I/O is the ability of a program to take a file as input or create a file as output.

blocks.title: open
bullets: `open` is a functionality built into Python that allows you to open a file and utilize it in your program:

blocks.title: open Example
blocks.code:
name = input("What's your name? ")

file = open("names.txt", "w")
file.write(name)
file.close()
blocks.expectedOutput: Run this code to see the result.

blocks.title: open
blocks.body: The `open` function opens a file called `names.txt` with writing enabled, as signified by the `w`.
bullets: Running this program multiple times will entirely rewrite the file each time. Ideally, we want to append. The `a` mode means "append":

blocks.title: open Example
blocks.code:
name = input("What's your name? ")

file = open("names.txt", "a")
file.write(f"{name}\n")
file.close()
blocks.expectedOutput: Run this code to see the result.

blocks.title: open
bullets: It's quite easy to forget to close the file.

blocks.title: with
bullets: The keyword `with` allows you to automate the closing of a file:

blocks.title: with Example
blocks.code:
name = input("What's your name? ")

with open("names.txt", "a") as file:
    file.write(f"{name}\n")
blocks.expectedOutput: Run this code to see the result.

blocks.title: with
bullets: What if we want to read from a file? Use `r` mode:

blocks.title: with Example
blocks.code:
with open("names.txt", "r") as file:
    lines = file.readlines()

for line in lines:
    print("hello,", line.rstrip())
blocks.expectedOutput: Run this code to see the result.

blocks.title: with
blocks.body: `readlines` reads all the lines of a file and stores them in a list. `rstrip` removes the extraneous line break at the end of each line.

blocks.title: CSV
bullets: CSV stands for "comma separated values".
Let's create `students.csv` with content like `Hermione,Gryffindor` on each line, and read it:

blocks.title: CSV Example
blocks.code:
with open("students.csv") as file:
    for line in file:
        row = line.rstrip().split(",")
        print(f"{row[0]} is in {row[1]}")
blocks.expectedOutput: Run this code to see the result.

blocks.title: CSV
blocks.body: `split` tells the interpreter where to find the end of each value.
bullets: The `split` function returns multiple values, so we can assign two variables at once:

blocks.title: CSV Example
blocks.code:
with open("students.csv") as file:
    for line in file:
        name, house = line.rstrip().split(",")
        print(f"{name} is in {house}")
blocks.expectedOutput: Run this code to see the result.

blocks.title: CSV
bullets: We can sort a list of dictionaries by a key:

blocks.title: CSV Example
blocks.code:
students = []

with open("students.csv") as file:
    for line in file:
        name, house = line.rstrip().split(",")
        students.append({"name": name, "house": house})

for student in sorted(students, key=lambda student: student["name"]):
    print(f"{student['name']} is in {student['house']}")
blocks.expectedOutput: Run this code to see the result.

blocks.title: CSV
blocks.body: We use a `lambda` function, an anonymous function, to tell `sorted` which key to sort on.
bullets: Our code is a bit fragile. If a value itself contains a comma (e.g., `"Number Four, Privet Drive"`), splitting on `,` breaks. Python's built-in `csv` library comes with a `reader`:

blocks.title: CSV Example
blocks.code:
import csv

students = []

with open("students.csv") as file:
    reader = csv.reader(file)
    for row in reader:
        students.append({"name": row[0], "home": row[1]})

for student in sorted(students, key=lambda student: student["name"]):
    print(f"{student['name']} is from {student['home']}")
blocks.expectedOutput: Run this code to see the result.

blocks.title: CSV
bullets: It's better design to bake the column names into the CSV file (a header row) and use a `DictReader`:

blocks.title: CSV Example
blocks.code:
import csv

students = []

with open("students.csv") as file:
    reader = csv.DictReader(file)
    for row in reader:
        students.append({"name": row["name"], "home": row["home"]})

for student in sorted(students, key=lambda student: student["name"]):
    print(f"{student['name']} is in {student['home']}")
blocks.expectedOutput: Run this code to see the result.

blocks.title: CSV
bullets: What if we want to write to a CSV file? Use `DictWriter`:

blocks.title: CSV Example
blocks.code:
import csv

name = input("What's your name? ")
home = input("Where's your home? ")

with open("students.csv", "a") as file:
    writer = csv.DictWriter(file, fieldnames=["name", "home"])
    writer.writerow({"name": name, "home": home})
blocks.expectedOutput: Run this code to see the result.

blocks.title: CSV
bullets: You can learn more in Python's documentation of [CSV](https://docs.python.org/3/library/csv.html).

blocks.title: Binary Files and PIL
bullets: A binary file is simply a collection of ones and zeros. This type of file can store anything, including music and image data.
There is a popular Python library called `PIL` that works well with image files. Animated GIFs are a popular type of image file that has many image files within it that are played in sequence.

blocks.title: Binary Files and PIL Example
blocks.code:
import sys

from PIL import Image

images = []

for arg in sys.argv[1:]:
    image = Image.open(arg)
    images.append(image)

images[0].save(
    "costumes.gif", save_all=True, append_images=[images[1]], duration=200, loop=0
)
blocks.expectedOutput: Run this code to see the result.

blocks.title: Binary Files and PIL
blocks.body: We import the `Image` functionality from `PIL`. The first `for` loop loops through the images provided as command-line arguments. The last lines save the first image and append a second image, creating an animated GIF.
bullets: You can learn more in Pillow's documentation of [PIL](https://pillow.readthedocs.io/).
